CHAPTER – I 
 
The Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that the Government has come up  with some important 
initiatives in the area of revival / restructure / closure of CPSEs. As the Committee 
gathers, the earlier mechanism involved the adminis trative Ministry / Department, the 
BRPSE, the BIFR and finally the approving authority , the Cabinet. This multiplicity of 
agencies involved delay in granting approval to rev ival plans and most of the revival 
proposals when finally approved would have already become redundant due to escalation 
of costs owing to the time over run. This vexed sit uation contributed to the further 
downfall of the sick / loss incurring and weak CPSEs involved.    
Para No 41 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 Now, as per the new system the administrative Minis tries will oversee the 
performance of its CPSEs based on the guidelines fo r”streamlining the mechanism for 
revival and restructuring of sick / incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector 
Enterprises: General principles and mechanism of re structuring” issued by DPE. Further, 
the Government has done away with the BRPSE and BIF R and AAIFR and they would 
stand abolished once the NCLT is constituted. The NCLT, provided for in the Companies 
Act, 2013, will henceforth be the sole entity to de cide upon the revival / restructure 
proposals of CPSEs. Also, the revival / restructure process has been rendered time bound. 
In this regard, the Committee observes that the ste p taken to put the administrative 
Ministry in charge of the monitoring of the health of their respective CPSEs is an 
appropriate decision as mid-course correction and o ther reformative measures can be 
taken swiftly without any time lapse as no third pa rty is getting involved. The Committee 
expects that all the lacunae which plagued the earl ier system will be eliminated in the 
new mechanism.   
Para No 42 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 The recommendations of erstwhile BRPSE were adviso ry in nature and final 
decision regarding acceptance of such recommendatio ns rested with the administrative 
Ministries/Departments. In order to streamline the multiple mechanism for revival of sick 
CPSEs, the Government approved on 7.10.2015 for win ding up of Board for 
Reconstruction of Public Enterprises (BRPSE). Accor dingly, the BRPSE was wound up 
vide notification dated 9 
th  November, 2015.  
 
 DPE has issued guidelines issued for revival/restr ucturing of CPSEs. The 
administrative Ministries/ Departments are empowere d and made responsible to monitor 
the health of CPSEs functioning under their control  and take timely redressal measures 
for revival/ restructuring/disinvestment of sick/lo ss making CPSEs with the approval of 
the competent authority in a time bound manner .    
1 

 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that the Finance Minister has made couple of important 
policy pronouncements – first, regarding disinvestm ent of Government share in CPSEs 
and second, on the disposal of fixed assets of the CPSEs identified for winding up / 
closure. The Department has submitted that a mechan ism has been structured to look into 
the operationalisation of the said announcements. The multitier structure has CCEA at the 
summit, NITI Aayog would identify the CPSEs and the  critical parameters for 
disinvestments / strategic sale. The CGD is to func tion as supervisory and 
recommendatory body and an EC to valuate the assets  of CPSEs concerned. The 
Committee has taken specific note of the submission  of DPE that this entire subject falls 
under the purview of the Department of Disinvestmen t. However, the Committee 
observes that the subject will have a profound bear ing on the CPSEs in the country and 
DPE should evince keen interest in the way things s hape up on this front. This is even 
more important considering that the very mandate of  DPE has been enhanced on these 
lines and, it being member in all the relevant Comm ittees of disinvestment, the 
Department has to make more holistic interventions on the issues / policies pertaining to 
CPSEs.   
Para No 49 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 DPE has noted the views of the Committee. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2 
 
 
 

CHAPTER–II 
The Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government's replies 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 The Committee note that while replying to the query  on Mid Term Review 
(MTR) of schemes during XII Five Year Plan, the Dep artment has restricted themselves 
by just submitting that no review has been undertak en.  The Committee observes that the 
Department while replying to the Committee should keep in mind that answers given to a 
Parliamentary Committee should be holistic and self -contained.   In the absence of a 
substantial reply, the Committee is precluded from comprehending the reason for not 
undertaking the MTR.  This information has to be provided to the Committee. 
 
Para No 15 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 
 The observations of the Committee are noted for co mpliance.  The Mid Term 
Review Schemes was earlier being done at the level of Planning Commission and it did 
not take place during XII 
th  Plan Period.  Hence, it was reported to the Commit tee that 
MTR for DPE schemes in XIIth Plan has not been undertaken. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
 

CHAPTER–III 
The Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted 
the replies of the Ministry and has asked the Ministry to review its replies 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that DPE claims that the CPSEs in India are performing to 
the best of their abilities in the prevailing econo mic scenario of declining commodity 
prices, reduced capital inflows into their economie s and increasing financial volatility. 
Even while taking the claim of DPE in its face valu e and acknowledging the fact that the 
Committee is not in knowledge of the performance of  all the CPSEs in India, the 
Committee cannot but share its observation that the  current status of all the 31 CPSEs 
under the Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) is sic k / incipient sick and weak as per 
DPEs guidelines for  ”Streamlining the mechanism fo r revival and restructuring of sick / 
incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector Enter prises: General principles and 
mechanism of restructuring”. Accordingly, the Commi ttee observes that the stand taken 
by DPE that CPSEs are performing well under the giv en conditions as status-quoits and 
wants the Department to adopt a new forward looking stance. 
Para No. 13 
Action Taken Replies 
 The performance of CPSEs as per Public Enterprises Survey 2014-15 is given 
below: 
 Total turnover/gross revenue from operations of al l CPSEs during 2014-15 stood 
at Rs.19.96 lakh crore compared to Rs.20.66 lakh cr ore in 2013-14 showing a reduction 
in turnover of 3.40%. Overall net profit of all 235  CPSEs during 2014-15 stood at 
Rs.1.03 lakh crore compared to Rs.1.28 lakh crore i n 2013-14 showing a decrease in 
overall profit of 19.71 %. The net worth of all CPS Es went up from Rs.9.45 lakh crore in 
2013-14 to Rs.9.85 lakh crore in 2014-15 registerin g a growth of 4.12 %. Contribution of 
CPSEs to Central Exchequer decreased from Rs.2.20 l akh crore in 2013-14 to Rs.2.00 
lakh crore in 2014-15 showing a decline of 9.23 %.  
 
 DPE has issued guidelines for revival/restructurin g of CPSEs. As per the 
guidelines, the administrative Ministries/ Departme nts are responsible to monitor the 
health of CPSEs functioning under their control and  take timely redressal measures for 
revival/ restructuring/disinvestment of sick/loss m aking CPSEs with the approval of the 
competent authority. 
 
Further Recommendations  
 
 The Committee finds that the reply of DPE has not a ddressed the concerns 
flagged by the Committee in its recommendation. DPE  should base their opinion on 
the actual individual performance status of CPSEs o n their own guidelines rather 
than echoing the macro performance details of the P ublic Enterprises Survey 2014-
15. Even from the performance figures provided by D PE from the Public 
Enterprises Survey, the Committee does not find jus tification for the sweeping 
opinion of DPE that all CPSEs in the country are pe rforming to the best of their 
abilities under the given circumstances.  
 
4 

 Accordingly, the Committee reiterates its recommen dation that the stand of 
DPE regarding the performance of CPSEs is status-qu oits and expects a more 
coherent response from DPE in this regard. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
5 

CHAPTER – IV 
Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry 
have not been  received 
 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that the mandate of DPE has be en augmented with the 
addition of roles in monitoring of performance of C PSEs and effective management of 
their assets.  This has been done by addition of su bjects to the Allocation of Business of 
DPE.  The Committee is of the considered opinion th at though the Budget allocation of 
DPE is small compared to the major Ministries/ Depa rtments of the Government, the role 
to be essayed by them is critical.  As the nodal De partment of all CPSEs in India, their 
effective evaluation and monitoring is going to be humongous task.  The newly added 
responsibility of CAPEX monitoring, measures to imp rove performance of CPSEs and 
other capacity building initiatives and advice rega rding revival/ restructuring/ closure of 
CPSEs will render the working of DPE pivotal to the way CPSEs perform in the country. 
Para No. 10 
Action Taken Replies 
 Department of Public Enterprises is compiling the C APEX of select CPSEs on 
monthly basis and submitting it in the prescribed format. 
 
 Department of Public Enterprises has issued MoU Gu idelines 2016-17 under 
which (i) “CAPEX” MoU parameter has been prescribed  as one of the mandatory targets 
for CPSEs with weightage of 15-20.  It has been fur ther explained that CAPEX may be 
decided on the basis of viable projects available f or expansion, modernisation or 
diversification, cash and bank balance or parked fu nds, net worth, borrowings etc., and, 
(ii) “CAPEX” under the title “Leveraging Net Worth”  has been prescribed as one of 
mandatory targets for CPSEs with weightage of 5-15. 
 
Further Recommendations/ observations 
 
 
 The Committee takes note of the fact that DPE has started compiling the 
CAPEX data of CPSEs. The Committee waits to be info rmed of the methodology 
adopted for the analysis of the above said data and  how DPE proposes to utilize the 
information so obtained with respect to the extant guidelines of the Department in 
this regard. 
 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 Accordingly, the Committee observes that DPE shoul d realize and imbibe the 
magnitude and importance of the responsibilities th at have been entrusted to them and 
take more proactive measures to play out this role.  Rather them imagining themselves 
just as a nodal coordinating agency. DPE should rei nvent themselves as an arm of the 
Government which can take decisive steps on its own  or in coordination with other 
Ministries / Departments to create a facilitative m ilieu for CPSEs to perform to their 
potential. The Committee is of the firm view that D PE should not be restricting 
themselves to just issuing guidelines and providing  advice. The new mandate gives them 
ample space to effectively follow up the implementation of the advices rendered by them  
6 

through their guidelines. Accordingly, the Committe e recommends that to be able to do 
this, DPE has to equip themselves better and come o ut with measures implementable on 
ground and also endeavour to create a coordinative platform involving the respective 
administrative Ministry and other relevant Governme nt agencies through which matters 
relating to the working of CPSEs in the country can  be resolved at a single stage availing 
time lag in administrative decisions, the single mo st degenerative factor in case of 
decisions related to CPSEs. 
Para No. 11 
Action Taken Replies 
 
 The observations/ recommendations of the Committee are noted. 
 
Further Recommendations/ observations  
 
 The Committee would wait for the information regar ding the concrete action taken 
by the Department regarding the setting up of a coordinative platform involving the 
respective administrative Ministries and other rele vant Government agencies 
through which matters relating to the working of CP SEs in the country can be 
resolved at a single stage.  
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 Further, from the submission of the DPE, the Commi ttee takes note that of the XII 
Plan outlays for various schemes of DPE, three sche mes have seen roughly around only 
50% of utilisation and one has seen only 20% of exp enditure.  The money allocated for 
Information Technology alone has seen a healthy uti lisation.   Here again, since a review 
of the scheme has not been undertaken the reasons f or the gross underperformance 
observed in the plan schemes are alien to the Commi ttee.  Regardless of this, the 
Committee expresses its dissatisfaction in the way of the plan schemes of DPE have 
underperformed during the XIIth Plan period. DPE sh ould make themselves aware of the 
reasons behind this situation and take necessary st eps to prevent them from recurring and 
report the same to the Committee. 
Para No 16 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 One of the reasons for underutilisation of XII th  Plan outlay of Plan Schemes of 
DPE is the decline in the targets CRR Scheme due to  gradual reduction in the VRS in 
CPSEs during the last few years.  Further, expendit ure under RDC, especially during 
2015-16, declined due to a change in MoU system by which the practice of constituting 
various ‘Task Force’ has been dispensed with.  However, now the RDC Scheme has been 
modified to extend its scope to include more activi ties such as thematic studies on the 
generic issues of general/ sectoral nature, seminar s and workshops to adopt collaborative 
and cooperative learning for experience  sharing, t raining programmes for capacity 
building and skill development, improvement in perf ormance evaluation and 
management processes of CPSEs, incentives best prac tices in focus areas through grant 
of awards/ incentives to CPSEs and SLPEs.  The broa dened arrangement will enhance 
utilisation of funds under the RDC Scheme.  Similar ly, in respect of CRR Scheme also, 
DPE has taken-up with National Skill Development Co rporation (NSDC) to broaden the 
network of training providers and to follow a stand ardized methodology of training 
design and delivery.  Broadening the network of training providers will help in covering  
7 

maximum possible number of VRS/CSS optees in future. 
 
 With the modifications introduced in the RDC Schem e and broadening of various 
areas/fields under its ambit, activities will be spread over the entire financial year to bring 
about effective utilisation of funds during 2016-17 and in the future. 
 
Further Recommendations/ observations 
 
 
 If VRS had reduced, the annual CRR allocation too s hould have been 
reduced accordingly, instead of retaining allocatio n despite under utilization. Also, 
DPE may inform about the alternative mechanism for ‘Task Force’ under MoU 
system. The Committee also recommends that outcome of studies, seminars, etc 
under RDC must be actionable initiatives that should be completed.  
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that departing from the pattern  of previous years, the 
Department has only two plan schemes in Financial Y ear 2016-17-Counselling, 
Retraining and Redeployment of Rationalized Employees of CPSEs (CRR) and Research, 
Development and Consultancy (RDC) on Generic issues  related to Enterprises (CPSEs & 
SLPEs).  A merger of schemes has been undertaken in  the case of RDC making the 
current RDC scheme more expansive containing more c omponents than earlier.  The 
Committee expects this measure to impart more finan cial and operational flexibility DPE 
resulting in better utilisation of allocated funds.  Accordingly, the Committee observes 
that DPE should make the most of the new initiative  brought out by the Ministry of 
Finance and avoid deficient utilisation and curtail ment of funds these schemes were 
prone to earlier. 
Para No 19 
Action Taken Replies 
 As mentioned in Para 16, RDC Scheme has been modif ied in the year 2016-17 
and the broadened arrangement will enhance utilisation of funds.  The observations of the 
Committee have been noted for compliance 
 
Further Recommendations/ observations 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed of the actionable out come of 
studies/seminars under RDC. 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee has always been appreciative of the objectives served by the CRR 
scheme which basically offers a social security net  to employees of CPSEs who optees 
for VRS or get retrenched. The Committee takes into  cognizance the fact that NIESBUD 
had undertaken an evaluation of the scheme in 2012- 13 and had recommended a host of 
improvements. One of the major recommendations was the need to stress more on 
follow-ups and redeployment after linking with micr o credit/finance. Handholding 
projects and linkages were also recommended to enha nce redeployment /self-
employment opportunities of the former employees an d their dependents trained under 
the scheme. DPE have submitted that there recommend ations had been circulated to the 
Nodal Agencies for compliance. However, Committee finds that the number of people  
8 

redeployed after being trained under the scheme has  always hovered around 50% or less 
of the total trained personnel. The situation has c ontinued even after the 
recommendations of NIESBUD made in 2012. Accordingl y, the Committee strongly 
recommends that the Department should take appropri ate measures expeditiously to 
improve the number of trainees who get redeployed s ubsequent to the training under the 
scheme. In this regard, the Committee also wants DP E to consider focussed Skill 
Development under current impetus accorded to skill  development by the Government. 
The Nodal Agencies under the Scheme should identify the skill sets that are in demand in 
the local area in terms of employability and provid e training to people under the Scheme. 
To the Committee, this is one of the measures that can be taken to improve the 
redeployment ratio. Further,  this will also contribute towards the efforts of th e 
Government to address the huge skill deficit of the  workforce in the country in different 
spheres. 
Para No 24 
Action Taken Replies 
  The Department has taken a note of the observations of the Committee to improve 
the number of trainees who get redeployed subsequen t to training under CRR Scheme. 
However, it may be appreciated that the target grou p of CRR scheme is very unique and 
quite distinct from other Schemes of the Government . Mostly the VRS/VSS optees 
belong to 45-50 years age group. Therefore, there c ould be constraints in micro 
credit/bank finance affecting the feasibility of hi gher rate of redeployment. The 
provisions regarding inclusion of dependents (in li eu of eligible VRS optee, if the optee 
himself is not coming forward) has given fillip to the scheme and as per recent trend 
coverage of dependents is 40% to 50%. 
 
  However, with a view to broaden the network of Noda l Agencies/Training 
Providers and also to follow standardized methodolo gy of training, design and delivery, 
DPE has taken up with National Skill Development Co rporation (NSDC) seeking their 
support for quality and market oriented skill devel opment training under the CRR 
Scheme through their empanelled Training Providers.  This is likely to facilitate a proper 
matching of individual skills, aptitude of the typi cal target group and help in augmenting 
redeployability under the CRR Scheme. 
 
Further Recommendations/ observations. 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed of the outcome of neg otiation with NSDC 
and also how will the CRR be redesigned.  
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee note that during 2015-16, with only a fortnight left for the 
completion of the Financial Year almost Rs 1 crore out of the total Rs. 2.81 crore 
allocated to the scheme at RE has been left unspent .  The Committee take exception to 
such underutilization under an important initiative  like RDC scheme. However, the 
Committee takes into account the hope expressed by DPE that from 2016-17 onwards the 
performance of the scheme is expected to improve as  it has seen broad basing of its 
objectives and new components have been added as pa rt of subsuming some other 
schemes into it. Further, the umbrella nature of th e scheme is thought to provide more 
financial interoperationability. This will also help the Department to tide over the earlier  
9 

problem of last quarter spending peculiar to the ea rlier RDC scheme for which the 
Ministry of Finance has already granted an exemption from spending limits. 
 Para No 28 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 Under RDC Scheme, the amount of Rs.71.01 lakh was s urrendered in 2015-16 
since MoU negotiation meetings could not be held an d therefore bills were not raised.  
This Department has taken a note of the suggestions  of the Committee to enhance 
utilisation of funds under RDC Scheme.   
 
 CSR Cell, DPE has planned to organize five seminar s/ conferences / workshops 
on Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) during 201 6-17 and would utilize the 
earmarked funds under RDC Scheme of DPE well within time.  
 
 The observations of the Committee have been noted. 
Further Recommendations/ observations. 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed of actionable outcome s of these 
seminars/conferences/workshops under RDC. 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee is happy to know that the Department  has already initiated steps 
to act on its recommendation regarding setting up o f a monitoring system to look into 
CSR fund utilisation by CPSEs.  It is also apprecia ted that the matter has also been taken 
up with the MoCA which administers the Companies Ac t, 2013.  The Committee 
observes that DPE should work in synchronisation wi th the MoCA in the matter relating 
to the monitoring of the CSR fund utilisation to en sure efficient internalisation of the 
CSR culture by CPSEs, thereby setting example for the private sector also to emulate. 
 
Para No 31 
Action Taken Replies 
 CSR Cell, DPE has collected sector-wise information  from CSR eligible CPSEs 
on utilization of CSR funds in order to monitor the  CSR spend by these CPSEs. Further, 
on all important issues relating to CSR provisions in the Companies Act, 2013, 
Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 and Schedule-VII  of the Act, DPE seeks advice of 
M/o Corporate Affairs.  
Further Recommendations/ observations. 
 
 
 DPE may include CSR performance on CPSEs in the Pu blic Enterprises 
Survey as a separate chapter. 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 Firstly, the Committee notes with dissatisfaction t he disowning by DPE of the subject 
matter related to the agencies involved in the revival / restructure / closure of CPSEs in India. The 
Committee is critical of the tendency of the Depart ment to compartmentalise the replies by 
contending that the role of NCLT and BIFR would be explained by the respective Ministry /  
10 

Department concerned. As the nodal Department for t he overseeing of all CPSEs in the country, 
DPE is expected to provide a cogent reply to the Co mmittee even if the subject matter falls under 
the domain of other Ministries / Departments / Agen cies. The responsibility of action on the 
subject being with another Ministry / Department / Agency can be justified, but that should not 
preclude the collection of information on the subject. 
Para No 40 
Action Taken Replies 
 Matter relating to dealing with sick CPSEs under C ompanies Act, 2013 which 
includes the role of different agencies in this reg ard was taken up with Ministry of 
Corporate Affairs (MoCA). 
 
 Ministry of Corporate Affairs has replied vide  OM No.17/40/2016CL.V dated 
18.3.2016 that Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”) vide  Section 407 to 434 (both inclusive), 
provide inter alia  for setting up of (a) the National Company Law Tri bunal (NCLT) and 
(b) the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NC LAT). The Act provides for 
revival and rehabilitation of sick companies which are enumerated in section 253 to 269 
of the Companies Act, 2013. However, since these se ctions are yet to be notified by 
MoCA, NCLT and NCLAT are yet to be operationalized. 
 
 At present, the Board of Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR / 
Appellate Authority for Industrial and Financial Re construction (AAIFR) are authorized 
in the Sick Industrial  Companies (SPECIAL PROVISIO NS) Act, 1965 for approval of 
revival & rehabilitation of Sick Companies including CPSEs.  
 
 Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MoCA) has also info rmed that the NCLT will 
replace (a) the existing Company Law Board (CLB), ( b) the Board of Industrial and 
Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) and (c) Appellate A uthority for Industrial and Financial 
Reconstruction (AAIFR) and (a) will also acquire th e jurisdiction of the High Courts in 
the matters where it is vested in the High Courts u nder the Act. Bodies referred at (b) and 
(c) will stand abolished upon notification of the SICA (Repeal) Act, 2003. 
 
 MoCA has further stated that the Insolvency and Ba nkruptcy Code, 2015 has been 
introduced in the Parliament and it proposes to ame nd the Companies Act, 2013 with 
regard to insolvency (revival as well as  winding up) related provisions also. 
 
Further Recommendations/ observations 
 
 
 The Committee expects to be informed about the prog ress made towards the 
operationalisation of National Company Law Tribunal  (NCLT) and the National 
Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) and reasons for the delay in this 
regard. Also, since the Insolvency and Bankruptcy C ode, 2016 has been assented to 
by the President in May, 2016 the Committee also wa nts to know the details of the 
consequential action taken/ to be taken regarding t he matter raised in the 
recommendation. 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 Further, it is observed that now with the enhanced mandate, DPE can also have a 
proactive role to play in the process. The NCLT has  been envisaged for all type of 
companies in India, not just CPSEs. In this scenario, the Committee recommends that  
11 

DPE has to take this into account and take appropri ate measures in coordination with the 
MoCA to ensure that the CPSEs, due to their particu lar requirements of meeting socio-
economic obligations, are not put at a disadvantage d position in their efforts to get 
revived / restructured as they would be treated as per the provisions of the Companies 
Act, 2013. 
Para No 43  
Action Taken Replies 
 DPE has noted the concerns of the Committee. The M inistry of Corporate Affairs 
has been informed to take note of the concern of th e Committee while formulating 
policies in this regard. 
 
Further Recommendations/ observations 
 
  
 The Committee wants to be informed of the progress made in this regard by 
DPE by pursuing the matter further with the MoCA. 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 Further, the Committee has always taken a firm stan d that the fixed assets, 
particularly land, of would up CPSEs should be reta ined with the Government or its 
agencies.  It is apprehended that the sale of such land to private players might have be 
potential to generate many unethical practices.  Ac cordingly, the Committee is of the 
strong and unanimous opinion that the land belongs to wound up CPSEs shall be retained 
with the Central Government or State Government or other Government agencies.  Since 
Secretary, DPE is the member of CGD it is firmly re commended that this view of the 
Committee should be emphatically placed before the CGD while formulating any policy 
in this area, for the present or in future.  The Secretary has agreed to place the view points 
of this Committee before CGD, when they deliberate on the approaches to be followed 
for disposal or usage of land which is in the hands  of sick PSEs or autonomous bodies.  
The committee sincerely hopes that the view point would be considered in CGD. 
Para No 50  
Action Taken Replies 
 Department of Investment and Public Asset Managemen t, which acts as the 
secretariat to the CGD, has been requested to inclu de the views of the Committee in the 
agenda of the next CGD meeting for its consideration vide DPE O.M. dated 06.06.2016. 
 
 DPE has conveyed the views/concerns of the Committ ee to the Secretary, 
Department of Investment and Public Asset Managemen t (erstwhile Department of 
Disinvestment) which act as a secretariat of the CG D vide O.M. dated 24.5.2016 with the 
approval of Secretary, DPE for placing the views of  the Committee before CGD for its 
consideration. 
 
Further Recommendations/ observations 
 
 
 The Committee wants to be updated of the progress m ade in this regard by 
the Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment  (CGD) and the final decision by the 
Government.

Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes with concern that none of the CPSEs under DHI have been 
found to be operating in a healthy manner.  The sta tus of CPSEs has been classified as 
weak, incipient sick or sick.  In the case of DHI, even the prestigious Maharatna BHEL 
has been termed as a ‘Weak’ CPSE. The Committee con siders this as an extremely 
alarming situation which calls for decisive interve ntion by DHI, the administrative 
department.  As per the New Guidelines of DPE, the primary responsibility for ensuring 
profitable functioning of CPSEs lies with the respe ctive administrative ministries.  In this 
regard, the Committee is aware that the Government has come up with a lot of new 
initiatives to reshape the avenues for revival /res tructure of CPSEs.  This includes the 
winding up of Board for Industrial and Financial Re construction (BRPSE), constitution 
of National Council of Law Tribunal (NCLT) and othe r similar measures.  The subject of 
revival /restructuring of CPSEs have repeatedly att racted the attention of the Committee 
and every time the Department comes up with some ge neralized reasons and solutions to 
the entire problem.  However, the Committee has fou nd that the lack of foresight and 
timely action can be termed as one of the main caus es for the poor plight of the CPSEs. 
In this scenario, the Committee would like to stron gly recommend that DHI desperately 
needs some workable roadmap on the performance of e ach of its 31 CPSEs regardless of 
their current classification.  It is also recommend ed that some appropriate mechanism for 
fixing responsibility with the management of the CP SEs for the distress of CPSE 
concerned has to be drawn up. 
Para No.54 
Action Taken Replies  
 
 The Department of Heavy Industry has started the p rocess of undertaking a fresh 
appraisal of the status of each CPSE with a view to  assessing the prospects of revival on 
case to case basis. As a part of this exercise, whi le profit making CPSEs require further 
strengthening, the loss making CPSEs having the pot ential of being turned around need 
to be revived.  Those CPSEs which have been chronic ally sick and are not found 
revivable on sustainable basis are to be disinveste d or closed after payment of due 
compensation to employees.

 As regards categorization of  BHEL as a “weak” CPS Es alongwith BHEL EML 
(Subsidiary of BHEL) the following background and factual position is placed before the 
Hon’ble Committee:- 
           
 (i) The reasons for decline in performance of CPSE s vary from enterprise to 
enterprise. The causes can be broadly classified in to two categories viz. (a) Internal 
causes, and (b) External causes. While ‘Internal ca uses’ are those which can be attributed 
to the management, the ‘External causes’ are those which are attributed to factors outside 
the purview / control of the management. The pace i s based on both internal and external 
factors. Some common issues associated with the dec line in performance and losses of 
CPSEs include old and obsolete plant and machinery,  outdated technology, low capacity 
utilization, excess manpower, weak marketing strate gies, stiff competition, dependence 
on Government orders, heavy interest burden, high i nput cost, resource crunch, change in 
Government policy, general economic conditions etc. As such, performance improvement 
of CPSEs with suitable interventions by the Governm ent is a continuous process, 
including facilitated by the Government Nominees an d Independent Directors on the 
Board of such CPSEs. Enterprise specific measures f or their turn around are taken and 
inter-alia include business restructuring, such as, formation of joint ventures, merger with 
another PSE, modernization and improved marketing s trategies, etc. Moreover, financial 
and non-financial targets for the CPSEs are fixed k eeping in view the prevailing business 
scenario through the mechanism of Memorandum of Und erstanding (MoU), which is a 
negotiated agreement signed between the Administrat ive Department/Ministry of the 
Government and the Management of the CPSEs. Achieve ment of targets is inter-alia 
dependent on sectoral business environment. Moreover, the performance of CPSEs under 
the administrative control of DHI is reviewed by the Department. 
 
 (ii) As regards BHEL being categorised as a “Weak”  CPSE as per the DPE 
Guidelines for “Streamlining the mechanism for revi val and restructuring of sick / 
incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector Enter prises: General principles and

not factor the operating business environment and t he severe competitive intensity faced

operations/ category/ sector. BHEL businesses being  a part of Capital Goods Industry

decrease in fresh executable orders maturing in the  market due to which there has been a

Para No.83

 With the funds made available to NPPC, it is state d that NPPC has already started

activities are in standstill from August 2015 due n on-availability of project fund. Since

further funds could not be released.  
 
Recommendation/ observation 

 
27 
 
 The Committee while taking into account the undue delay on the part of the 
Government/ BIFR, is equally disappointed that NPPC  could not utilize the funds 
allocated in 2013-14 timely and also could not prod uce the Utilization Certificate for the 
same which curtailed allocation of funds thereafter . Here, the Committee observes that 
the funds for revival of CPSEs are provided by the Government after a long fought 
approval process.  In this individual case, after a  long drawn process of approval and 
sanctioning of fund, the management of NPPC has failed squarely to make best use of the 
funds.  As per the new guidelines of DPE for reviva l/restructuring of CPSEs, the 
administrative ministry has the primary responsibil ity regarding the health of its CPSEs.

management of NPPC in the implementation of the rev ival plan and see to that they steer 
clear of such lapses in the times ahead. 
Para No.84 
Action Taken Replies  
 In addition to the facts mentioned above in point no.23. It is also stated that NPPC 
has now submitted a profitability statement with ad ditional Rs.372 crore of Revised Cost

Further Recommendations 
 
 
 
The Committee takes note of the replies of the Gove rnment with regard to 
the revival/restructuring of NPPC. Foremost, the De partment states that the long 
drawn delay in the implementation of the revival of  NPPC has been largely due to 
the delay caused by BIFR, the approval having been received only in January, 2015. 
However, the Committee finds that the delay has con tinued to plague NPPC even 
after that. The amount of Rs 100 crore released for  the purpose of revival of NPPC 
could not be utilised completely and non-production  of utilization certificates 
precluded further allocation of funds. However, the  Department has failed to 
mention why the company has not been able to produce Utilisation Certificate. Since 
non –submission of Utilisation Certificate is the o nly valid reason stated to the 
Committee for this situation, it is felt that NPPC is solely responsible for the stalling 
of revival activities since August, 2015.  
 
 Further, the Department in their reply has made a one line statement that a 
profitability statement has been submitted by NPPC with a Revised Cost Estimate. 
The Committee finds such one liners without any exp lanation on such important 
issues as most unacceptable and would like to remin d the Department that any 
submission made before a Parliamentary Committee sh ould be cogent and well 
explained. Accordingly, the Committee strongly reco mmends that the Government, 
atleast at this stage, should adopt a serious appro ach to the revival/restructuring of 
NPPC and submit a comprehensive reply to its recomm endations and further 
observations of the Committee. 
 

 
28 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that HNL has taken efficient a nd practical steps aimed at 
revival of the Company. These proactive steps are e xpected to bring down the production 
cost of newsprint and provide HNL a comparative adv antage in the market.  The 
Committee observes that the steps adopted by Govern ment of Kerala are highly 
supportive of the cause of HNL and the management o f HNL would do well to make 
efficient use of it.  Further, it is recommended th at alongwith cost cutting measures HNL 
should also revisit its marketing strategies to be able to fully translate the benefits brought 
by the expected cost advantage to tangible financial gains for the company.  
Para No.87 
Action Taken Replies  
 
 HNL has been advised accordingly. 
 
Further Recommendations 
 
 
 The Committee notes that DHI has advised HNL regard ing the 
recommendation of the Committee. However, the Commi ttee also wants to be 
updated about the specific measures adopted by HNL in this regard. Whether NITI 
Aayog has given any recommendation on HNL and the v iews of the Ministry 
thereon?  
 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 As informed by DHI the Company is expected to turn  around after a three-year 
streak of losses.  In this regard, it is expected t hat DHI will monitor and guide HNL step

in a position to substitute imported material. In v iew of this, the Committee recommends 
that DHI should proactively take up the duty ration alizations requested by HNL with the 
appropriate agencies. 
        Para No.88 
Action Taken Replies  
 
 This would be considered separately. 
 
 
Further Recommendations 
 
 
 The reply of the Government does not specify wheth er rationalisation of 
customs duty as requested by HNL has been taken up by the Department 

 
29 
 
appropriately.  The Committee wants to have a more complete reply regarding the

turnaround expected to be achieved by HNL.   
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 As per the facts placed before the Committee it is  noted that the RMDP of NEPA

           Para No.95

 As regards RMDP of Nepa, it is likely to be comple ted by March 2017. DHI is

 The Committee considers the reply of the Government  regarding NEPA to

covering every aspect of the recommendation.  Wheth er NITI Aayog has given any

Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee’s observation after hearing the repr esentatives of Auto & Capital 
Goods Sector associations is that the need of the h our is to focus more on urban & rural 
infrastructure, road & highways, satellite cities, etc to generate demands at home in both 

 
30 
 
these sectors. For auto industry, the Committee is of the opinion that they should start 
looking for export markets in the face of saturatin g domestic arena while formulating

technology in the field of electric vehicles. CG as sociations should come up with a 
concrete plan in tune with the NCGP, 2016 objective s of the Government to triple the

Para No.100 
Action Taken Replies  
 
 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted for compliance. 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee takes into account through the submi ssion of DHI that they have 
already taken into cognizance the areas put forth b y the industry associations seeking 
attention of the Government. Nevertheless, the Comm ittee recommends that the 
Government should look into the issues submitted by  these associations before the

Para No.101 
 
Action Taken Replies 
                                        Capital Sector 
 
 As far as Capital Goods sector is concerned, the d epartment has undertaken

sector.  The different schemes will help in realizi ng the vision of “Building India as a

(ii) 
 
 
 
 
 

 
REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises on the recommendations contained in the 
Committee’s Two Hundred Seventy Fifth Report on Dem ands for Grants (2016-17)  
pertaining to the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
 
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises in respect of the recommendation s contained in the Report. These have 
been categorized as follows:  
 
Chapter –I   The recommendations/observations, which have bee n accepted by the 
Ministry. 
 
 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report. 
 
Chapter -II   The recommendations/observations which the Commit tee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government's replies. 
 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic and 
explanations advanced by the Ministry and therefore  do not want to pursue them for the 
present. 
 
Chapter -III    The recommendations/observations in respect of w hich the Committee has 
either not accepted replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its reply. 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-i mplementation of 
recommendations contained in Chapter – III and desi res that the Ministry should furnish 
logical explanations therefor. 
 
Chapter -IV    The recommendations/observations in respect of wh ich final replies of the 
Ministry have not been received. 
 
 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has either 
furnished the interim replies or couched its langua ge in vague terms like noted for 
compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee desir es that the Ministry should furnish 
Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendations c ategorized in Chapter-IV in detail and 
to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee. 
 
3. The details of the ATR are being discussed in the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
 

-2- 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
It  is  evident  that  every  year  since  2013-14  the  Planned  allocation  has 
remained significantly under utilized by every wing  of the Ministry. And 
considering the expenditure norms prescribed by the  Ministry of Finance that not 
more than 33% of BE can be spent in last quarter of  FY and not more than 15%  
of  BE  can  be  spent  in  the  month  of  March  of FY,  it is  unlikely  that 
Ministry can stick to these norms this year (2015-1 6) as well and, therefore, 
unlikely to utilize the available resources prudent ly.  In the financial year 2015-16 
too,  as  per  the E-lekha  of  Controller  General   of  Accounts,  only  67%  of 
Planned allocation was spent by the end of January 2016, however, as per the 
above information provided  by the Financial  Advis or of the Ministry, about 
96% of Planned BE was likely to be spent by the end  of FY 2015-16 and around 
29% of the Planned BE was spent in last two months.     
   
  (Para 14) 
Action Taken :  
 
  It is true that expenditure of Plan allocation was relatively less during 
the year 2015-16 but it has considerably improved in 2016-17. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee considers these Schemes a reflection of inadequate planning 
and poor implementation. Norms of Schemes are delay ed and schemes are  
modified  the  mid-way  and  till  the  modified  n orms  are  finalized  and 
approved by the competent authority, the allocation  remains frozen. 
(Para 22) 
 
Action Taken :  
 
The observations of the Committee are noted. All th e schemes are 
implemented as per the schemes guidelines, which ar e reviewed from time to time. 
 
 
 

-3- 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
In view of 345 lakh unregistered units in the count ry as per Fourth Census 
conducted in 2006-07, registration of mere 4 lakh u nits is rather slow and tardy 
progress. The very fact that of 4 lakh registration s majority are micro and small 
entrepreneurs, shows great demand among these entre preneurs to register to 
avail of possible benefits of Government schemes.   It is also evident that in 
certain smaller, hill and remote States, the regist ration has not picked up. Even in 
larger States the progress in registration is slow compared to the scope and 
extent of this Sector. The Committee recommends tha t it will require a sustained 
campaign to register all the MSMEs under UAM and th at the registration must be 
linked with benefits.  
(Para 40) 
Action Taken:  
 
For utilization of the Udyog Aadhaar Programme, the  notifications issued in this 
regard has been uploaded in the website of this Min istry. A national web portal 
namely, http://udyogaadhaar.gov.in has also been la unched for enabling e-filing of 
Udyog Aadhar Memorandum.  States have been requeste d to issue instructions to 
the concerned Directors of industries and General M anagers of DIC for expeditious 
implementation of UAM.  In the regional meetings, S tates were requested to 
undertake steps to encourage UAM registration. The benefit of Udyog Aadhar 
Memorandum registration is ease in registering the unit and getting benefits from 
the scheme/programme run by the Government.  As of now, the registration has 
crossed 11 lakhs and, on an average, more than 4000  MSE units are getting 
registered every day. The process was, so far, slow  because of systemic  issues 
which technology has resolved.     
  
Recommendation/Observation  
The Committee apprehends that even the ASPIRE may m eet the same 
fate  as  other  entrepreneurship  development  pro grammes  being  run  by  the 
Ministry. The Committee notes that ASPIRE too is fo llowing the set stereotypes 
of considering MSMEs as low cost low technology ent erprises, that may not 
independently survive the market competition   in l onger run. The Committee 
was surprised to note that as per the Fourth Census  of MSME 2006-07, out of 
the 15 lakh registered MSME units, about 5 lakh bec ame sick. And the trades 
that are offered under ASPIRE may not improve the s ituation. ASPIRE needs to 
break this stereotype and consider MSMEs as technol ogy intensive sector that 
can survive the market competition. 
(Para 159) 
 

-4- 
 
Action Taken :  
 
 The suggestion is noted and would be followed up. However, it is the 
intention of the ministry to break the stereotype u nder the ASPIRE scheme. The 
scheme provides the much needed space for technolog y innovation and rapid 
prototyping option, which could bring the technolog ies to the market through 
commercialization under the TBI component.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

-5- 
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
Recommendations/Observations which the Committee do es not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government’s replies 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
Also, Infrastructure Development and capacity build ing includes Tool  
Rooms that are essentially training institutions an d must not be clubbed with Office 
construction. Tool Rooms and Technology Centers can  be clubbed with Skill 
Development Programmes. And the Cluster Development  may be clubbed with 
SFURTI. 
(Para 8) 
Action Taken :   
 
 It is true that Tool Rooms have separate functions and their monitoring needs 
to be more regular. That is what is happening also.   Technology Centres are being 
monitored separately and construction of office bui lding is monitored separately.  
As far as cluster development is concerned, the ind ustrial cluster development is 
different form SFURTI cluster development because u nder SFURTI, the Ministry 
promotes only artisan cluster. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The  Committee  notes  that  while  all  the  wings   have  under-utilised  the 
available  resources,  the utilization  by SME Divi sion and the DC-MSME  has 
been particularly alarming. 
(Para 15) 
Action Taken:  
 
 The issue of underutilization of the available reso urces has been brought to 
the notice of the Ministry.  The Ministry has taken  it in the right earnest and it has 
improved its performance during the year 2016-17. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The   Committee   notes   a   marginal   increase   in   overall   Non-Planned 
allocation in RE 2015-16 and would like to know the  reasons as to why Non- 
Planned allocation for DC-MSME was reduced and that  of ARI and SME was 
increased. 
(Para 17) 

-6- 
Action Taken:  
 
 The Non Plan RE allocation is done by Ministry of Finance keeping in view 
of expenditure done by each Division on pro-rata. The Expenditure figures of 
DC(MSME) for Non Plan up to Sep 2015 (six months) w as Rs. 65.67cr, so 
accordingly the RE was fixed at RE Rs. 116.61 cr.  BE was Rs. 124.33 cr. And 
expenditure was Rs. 115.92 cr.  
 
BE for Non Plan for Ministry was Rs. 394.91cr where as expenditure was Rs. 
398.50 cr. Which is within RE of Rs. 400.86 cr.   
 
The Non-Plan RE for 2015-16 in respect of ARI & SME  was enhanced on 
account of (i) number of Pensioners increased, (ii)  Two D.A. installments of 10% 
each announced and (iii) implementation of MACP. No t all these factors can always 
be guessed/ estimated correctly.  DC(MSME), because  of its large workforce could 
estimate the figures in a better manner.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee notes massive gap between Planned Rev enue and Capital 
sections. While Total of Revenue section Planned an d Non-Planned is Rs 3140 
crores and that of Capital Section is mere Rs 10.55  crores.  However, these figures 
change dramatically in terms of Planned and Non-Pla nned allocations. Whereas 
total Planned allocation is Rs 3000 crores, the tot al Non Plan is Rs. 464.77 
crores.  The  Ministry  may  explain  how  does  it   reconcile  these  four 
different sets of figures that convey diametrically  opposite scenario. 
(Para 28) 
Action Taken:  
 
Planned Revenue, Capital, Plan and Non Plan allocat ion, all the four are 
different allocation. Plan allocation comprises of Plan Revenue and Capital 
expenditure for meeting the expenditure under vario us object heads of schemes of 
the Ministry of MSME. Non Plan allocation is meant for meeting the establishment 
expenditure of the organization under Ministry of M SME. There is no relation 
between Planned Revenue and Capital Section and als o Plan and Non Plan 
allocation.  This Department does have mostly GIA a nd Subsidies rather than 
Loans.  All the GIA & subsidies are taken in revenu e side so Expenditure on capital 
side is less.  Most of the plan expenditure is done  in Revenue Section because of 
GIA & Subsidies. Plan expenditure has no one-to-one  relation/mapping with either 
capital or revenue. And, a Ministry dealing with MS ME sector cannot have much 
requirement of capital expenditure. The Total Provi sions under GIA & Subsidies 
was Rs.1484.13 crore & Rs.1479.01crore respectively in this year. 

-7- 
 
However, under the Micro Units Development & Refina nce Agency Ltd. 
(Mudra) Yojana, the maximum loan amount is Rs. 10 l akhs which is less than the 
Bank loan component of unit under PMEGP Scheme so i t might not be possible for 
financing bank loan component of a PMEGP project un der MUDRA Yojana. 
However, MUDRA authorities have been provided with the web-link of KVIC, 
wherein the data pertaining to Trainees of various skill development programme and 
beneficiaries under PMEGP have been uploaded. The r equired data can be accessed 
and downloaded by the SIDBI for providing financial  assistance to projects of upto 
Rs.10 lakhs. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
The  Committee  wonders  that  a  scheme  for  MSME   start  ups  is  not 
assigned to the Ministry of MSME and is being imple mented through SIDBI.  As 
the Committee had sought to know the details and st ructure of SMILE Scheme for 
start ups being implemented by the SIDBI, same was not provided. The Committee 
seeks details of structure and performance of SMILE  Scheme. The Committee 
notes that the Ministry has been asking for more al location for PMEGP. The 
Committee may be informed if the schemes like PMEGP  and incubators under 
ASPIRE could be linked to SMILE.  
(Para 52) 
Action Taken:   
 
SIDBI has formulated SMILE Scheme with an objective  to provide soft loan, 
in the nature of quasi-equity and term loan on rela tively soft terms to MSMEs to 
meet the required debt-equity ratio norm for new un its as also for pursuing 
opportunities for growth by existing MSMEs. The sch eme is to take forward GoI’s 
‘Make in India’ campaign and to help MSMEs take part in the campaign.  
• All new as well as existing MSME units covered unde r 25 sectors covered under 
‘Make In India’ Programme of Government of India an d few other sectors are 
eligible under SMILE. 
Special features of SMILE: 
• It is a project finance scheme; wherein, MSMEs are assisted by way of soft loan, 
which is a quasi-equity assistance to meet the requ ired debt-equity ratio and term 
loan on relatively soft terms.  
• Maximum eligible quantum under soft loan is 10% of the project cost subject to a 
maximum of Rs. 20 lakh. A higher soft loan of up to  15% of the project cost will 
be considered for the enterprises promoted by Sched uled Caste (SC) / Scheduled 
Tribe (ST) / Persons with Disabilities (PwD) and wo men, subject to a maximum 
of  Rs. 30 lakh.     

-8- 
 
• Minimum term loan size is Rs. 25 lakh.                     
• While the interest rates are fixed based on rating of the proposal, the scheme 
provides concession in interest rate during the fir st 3 years from the date of first 
disbursement. Presently, the applicable interest ra te for initial period of three 
years is 9.35% p.a. for soft loans and interest rat es for term loan under SMILE 
ranges from 9.45% to 9.95% p.a., depending on the i nternal rating of the 
borrower.  
• The soft loan is converted into term loan after 3 y ear period and would carry rate 
as per the internal credit rating of term loan assigned at the time of sanction.   
• Longer moratorium period of upto 2 years will be provided for soft loan. 
• The scheme had benefitted 419 MSMEs with cumulative  sanctions of Rs. 1323 
crore till May 31, 2016. 
1. SIDBI operates Startup Assistance Scheme out its ow n resources, wherein startup 
ventures with revenue traction of at least 6 months  and subject to compliance of 
the norms under the Scheme are extended financial assistance by way of loans. 
As on March 31, 2016, SIDBI has assisted 57 Startup s with aggregate sanctioned 
amount of  Rs. 57.48 Crore under Startup Assistance  Scheme. The Scheme does not 
cover PMEGP whereas ASPIRE is meant for rural startups by way of equity through 
AIFs. 
 
The objective of SMILE Scheme  of SIDBI is to provide soft loan, in the 
nature of quasi-equity, and term loan on relatively  soft terms to MSMEs to meet the 
required debt-equity ratio for establishment of an MSME as also for pursuing 
opportunities for growth for existing MSMEs.  The minimum term loan will be Rs.50 
lakh for new enterprise and Rs.25 for existing ente rprises going for additional 
investment.  The minimum contribution of the promot er is 15% of the project cost 
for projects upto Rs.1 crore and 20% for the rest.  Term loan will be 75% for 
enterprises with total project cost upto to Rs.1 crore and 2/3 of the project cost for the 
rest, Soft loan will be 10% of the project cost sub ject to a minimum of Rs.20 lakh 
and upto 15% for enterprises promoted by SC/ST/PwD and women subject to a 
maximum of Rs.30 lakhs.  
Whereas the objectives of PMEGP  is aimed at generating self-employment 
opportunities through establishment of micro-enterp rises in the non-farm sector by 
helping traditional artisans and unemployed youth. General category beneficiaries 
can avail of margin money subsidy of 25% of the pro ject cost in rural areas and 15% 
in urban areas. For beneficiaries belonging to spec ial categories such as scheduled 
caste/scheduled tribe /women the margin money subsidy is 35% in  rural  areas  and  

-9- 
 
25% in urban areas. The maximum cost of projects is  Rs.25 lakh in the 
manufacturing sector and Rs.10 lakh in the service sector.  The assistance under 
PMEGP scheme is available only to new projects. 
The objectives of ASPIRE  scheme is to accelerate entrepreneurship and to 
promote start-ups for innovation and entrepreneursh ip in agro-industry through 
setting up of Incubators by providing one-time gran t of cost of Plant & Machinery.  
Whereas SMILE is for promoting individual enterprises. 
 
Similarly, on comparing PMEGP with SMILE, following observations may be 
drawn: 
 
1. The project cost under SMILE is from Rs. 50-100 lak hs whereas under 
PMEGP the project cost is limited to Rs.25 lakh only. 
2. Under SMILE, assistance of Rs.25 lakh is available for existing enterprises for 
upgradation whereas PMEGP scheme is available for new enterprises. 
In view of the above, PMEGP, ASPIRE and SMILE schem es are catering to 
different segments and hence cannot be linked or inter-linked.

Action Taken:   
 
Availment of refinance by Banks, RRBs and MFIs had picked up in last part 
of FY 2016 viz. during February/March 2016.  As on March 31, 2016, MUDRA had 
sanctioned refinance assistance amounting to Rs. 37 83.20 crore, out of which 
Rs.3337.20 crore has been disbursed to 16 PSU Banks , 3 RRBs and 21 Micro 
Finance Institutions.  Although RBI has allowed exe mption from Credit 
Concentration norms in respect of refinance assista nce to Scheduled Commercial 
Banks, the same is not exempted in respect of other  partner institutions.  Hence, 
MUDRA’s refinance to MFIs/NBFCs are subject to sing le party exposure norm of 
15% of Owned Fund, which works out to Rs.112.50 cro re.  Similarly, MUDRA is 
also subject to group exposure norm of 25% of Owned  Fund, which works out to 
Rs. 187.50 crore.  Moreover, Rs.250 crore sanctione d to 3 NBFCs could not be 
disbursed, as  MUDRA’s  assistance  to  NBFCs  is  subject to an interest cap of 6%

Action Taken:  
 
 As per RBI guidelines on Priority Sector Lending an d Classification dated

responsibility of the Ministry and the KVIC to prot ect and promote the reputation of

implement the PMEGP scheme. Accordingly guidelines for online transfer of 
PMEGP Margin Money funds directly to Financing Bank  Branches have been

 The Committee may be informed of the number of PME GP projects that

Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee considers this to be a violation of n orms prescribed by the 
Ministry of Finance, that money that should have be en spent evenly within that 
Financial Year, is allowed to remain unspent in the  subordinate offices  and  carried   
forward  to  next  Financial  year.  The Committee  may  be  informed whether the

Action Taken: 
  
 
As per the instructions of Ministry of Finance the Unspent Balance on a cutoff 
date should normally be worked out on the basis of the amount that has been 
released by the Ministry by that date and the amoun t for which requisite 
confirmation of actual utilization for intended pur poses has not been received by the 
Ministry by that date.  If the confirmation has not  been received, the total amount 
released should prima facie be taken as ‘unspent’ a s far as the Ministry is concerned.  
A  statement  of  unspent  balance  regularly  forwarded  to  Ministry  of  Finance  on  
quarterly basis. As per GFR 212(1) The utilization certificate should be submitted 
with in twelve month of the closure of the financia l year by the Institution or 
Organisation concerned.  If any grantee Institute o r any organization do not submit 
all the Utilization certificates (s) due for rendit ion in respect all of the 
Scheme/Programmes/Project then further grant is not  released to that grantee 
Institute/organization by the office of . 
 Next proposal for release of funds is processed du ly considering unspent 
balance lying with the Implementing Agencies under relevant Scheme Head.  
However, the recommendation of the Committee has be en noted and approval of the 
competent authority will be obtained to carry the m oney forward to the next financial 
year. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee recognizes that Ministry has not been  taking due 
approval of competent authority to carry money forw ard to next Financial

-86- 
Recommendation/Observation  
The Committee therefore wonders that if the previou s information given in

Action Taken:   
 
Regarding Plan S&T and Coir Vikas Yojana (CVY), the  Board could utilize 
the entire amount including opening balance and the  fund releases.  The Board has

However, the utilization under CUY has not picked u p due to reluctance on the part 
of the Bank to release loans to the applicants and under the component SCSP & TSP 
there is a slow pace of expenditure due to lesser i ntakes from the SCSP and TSP 
category. Since the utilization under these compone nts is not utilized at the desired 
level, the funds have been re-appropriated from CUY to CVY.   
 
 
The allocation was reduced due to slow pace of expe nditure and reluctance on 
the part of the Bank to release loans to the applic ants resulted in slow progress of the 
scheme and non-receipt of viable proposals.  Accord ingly, the Plan allocation was 
reduced from Rs.20 crore to Rs.8.38 crore under Coi r Udyami Yojana. Similarly, 
under Grant-in-Aid Salaries (Non-Plan) Head, budget  allocation of Rs.22.20 crore 
was reduced to 19.40 crore owing to the fact that t he utilization was 50% of the BE 
2015-16 upto September 2015.  As per M/o Finance’s norms, 7 months salary should 
have been disbursed upto September whereas 6 months  salary was released upto 
September.  On the basis of this, M/o Finance reduc ed the budget under Grant-in-Aid 
Salaries (Non-Plan) Head on pro-rata basis. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee feels that overall utilization by Co ir Board has been 
comparatively better.  Even in case of Coir Udyami Yojna, the Board could 
utilize the opening balance.  Therefore, there was no reason to reduce allocation 
in RE on the basis of under-utilization.  The Commi ttee fails to understand how 
could Non-Planned Grants in Aids (Salary) could be reduced which is a 
Committed obligation.  The Committee may be informe d of circumstances that 
led to violation of Ministry of Finance norms by Coir Board. .  
 

-87-

Funds meant for MDA to Non Planned Funds for paymen t of salaries. This was

to pay the salaries and that is why the Committee h as been arguing that the Ministry

making a lumpsum Non-Planned allocation for salarie s and other dues. However, in 
the instant case the Committee may be informed of the conditions that forced the 
Coir Board to divert Planned funds for the payments of salaries. Did the Coir

 It appears that for long the Coir Board suffered s hortage of Non-

-89- 
Recommendation/Observation  
The Committee is unconvinced with the reply about u nder-utilisation of

The Committee may be informed of the conditions whe re even such committed 
liabilities were under-utilised by the Coir Board w hich inter alia warranted a 
reduction of Non-Planned allocation at RE stage. 
(Para 228) 
Action Taken:  
 
The reason for reduction of Non-Plan allocation at RE stage was release of 6 
months salary i.e. 50% of the BE 2015-16 whereas the M/o Finance’s norms stipulate 
that 7 months salary should have been disbursed upt o September.  Accordingly, M/o

Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee has not been informed the circumstan ces for such breach

Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee may be informed about actual procedur e of devolution of 
subsidy to CUY beneficiary and the time taken in ac tual disbursal of subsidized 
loan. 
(Para 230) 
Action Taken:   
 
Coir Board invites the application for availing ass istance under Coir Udyami 
Yojana through the Board’s online portal – coirserv ices.gov.in.  One who desires to 
apply for assistance under CUY can register their a pplications through this portal at 
anytime from any part of the country.   The Field O ffices of the Board situated at 
different parts of the country will accept the onli ne applications coming under their 
jurisdiction.  The Officer-in-charge of the Field Office will scrutinize the applications 
and the applications which are complete in all respect will be referred to the Regional 
Level Selection Committee (RLSC) for its considerat ion. This should be done within 
21 days from the date of receipt of the application .  The Field Office will forward the 
applications recommended by the RLSC to the Financi ng Banks within 7 days of 
approval of RLSC. Once the application is received by the Financing Bank, the Bank  
 

-90- 
 
shall intimate the sanction of loan or otherwise to  the beneficiary and Coir Board 
within 30 calendar days.  On receipt of loan sancti on letter from the Financing Bank, 
the beneficiary shall deposit his contribution with in 30 calendar days to the 
concerned Bank.  The Bank shall release 1 
st  installment of loan to the beneficiary 
within 30 days of receipt of beneficiary contributi on.  The applicant should have 
undergone Entrepreneurship Development Programme be fore releasing the 1 st  
installment of loan by the Bank.  After receipt of the loan sanction letter and Margin 
Money Claim from the Financing Bank, the Field Offi ce shall submit these 
documents to Coir Board Head Office through online portal for sanction and release 
of Margin Money (Subsidy).  Coir Board Head Office shall process these online 
Margin Money Claims and intimate sanction or otherw ise to the Field Offices within 
7 days of receipt of the M.M Claims.  Within 3 days  of sanction of Margin Money 
(Subsidy), the Coir Board HO shall release the Marg in Money to the CUY Nodal 
Bank and the CUY Nodal Bank shall transfer the Marg in Money to the Financing 
Banks for depositing as TDR in the name of the beneficiary for two years.  To depict  
the devolution of Margin Money to the CUY beneficia ry the Board has prepared a 
Flow Chart indicating the time schedule, which is also annexed.  
 The actual disbursal of subsidized loan under the Scheme takes place within 
120 to 150 days.

 The Committee may be informed of total application s received during 
last year 2015-16, number of applications cleared b y RLSC and of those how 
many have been cleared by Banks.  Please provide Ba nk-wise details.  How 
many applications have actually been disbursed in 1 50 days.  Though the 
Committee feels that 150 day limit must be reduced to 100 days. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The  Committee  may  also  be  informed  about  the   purpose  of  proposed 
modification in the CUY Scheme. 
(Para 231) 
Action Taken:   
 
During the Scheme implementation, the Board felt th at continuation of Coir 
Udyami Yojana during the XII Plan period with modif ications is essential for 
adoption of modern technology in the production and  processing of coir which will 
facilitate improvement in quality, improving the ma rketing opportunities thereby 
enhancing  the  earning  capacity  of the workers. The Scheme will be highly suitable  

-91- 
 
for contributing to the development of vulnerable s ections of the society especially 
the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and peopl e in North Eastern Region.  
Coir Board has conducted an independent evaluation of the implementation of the 
scheme during the XI Plan period by engaging M/s. D atamation Consultants Pvt. 
Ltd., New Delhi. In the evaluation report it was me ntioned that the purpose of the 
Scheme towards rejuvenation has been immensely serv ed.  Further, the evaluators 
have recommended for continuation of the Scheme wit h focus on extensive 
modernization and to keep the Scheme open to all ca tegories in the coir sector 
enhancing the limit of the project cost to Rs.10 la khs. Streamlining of the Scheme to 
ease Banking process for the disbursement of the lo an and subsidy, deregulation 
machine procurement so that the beneficiary has the  freedom to purchase the 
machines of their choice were also their recommenda tions. A marketing plan to 
increase the sales was also recommended to be incor porated in the scheme as this 
would lead to a chain of events as increase in sales will lead increase in production as  
well as exports and for that more coir workers woul d be needed and these changes 
will lead to employment as well as income generation. 
 
Planning Commission’s Working Group on MSME Growth for XII Plan in its 
recommendations has also stressed the need for cont inuation of the scheme during 
XII Plan period with suitable modifications and exp ansion to cover manufacturing 
units for value added products and processes, using  high-end machines and 
technologies.  The Working Group has recommended fo r enhancement of the ceiling 
of the financial assistance under the scheme so as to cover small and medium scale 
units who will be able to absorb higher investments , besides continuing the benefits 
for the tiny work sheds and spinning units.   
 
On the basis of the above recommendations, the Boar d has proposed the 
modifications in the Scheme of Coir Udyami Yojana. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 It was informed that Banks are reluctant to financ e under CUY Scheme 
despite being supported by the Government.  The Com mittee may be informed 
of reasons to reluctance on the part of Banks and s teps taken to improve 
implementation.   
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee appreciates that the new modified MPD A scheme has 
enhanced the financial assistance to artisans to 40 % while reducing the share of 
producing and selling institutions. The Committee a pprehends if such reduction may 
become a dis-incentive for producing and selling un its. The Committee may also be  
 

-92- 
 
informed how does the Ministry calculate the per da y per artisan 
wage for   the   
purposes   of   overall   allocation   for   MPDA.   The   Committee   also 
recommends that the Ministry must explore the ways to transfer the wages directly 
to the Bank accounts of the artisan through DBT as is being done in other DBT

(Para 242) 
Action Taken:   
 
 Existing Market Development Assistance (MDA) schem e on production 
(Khadi & Poly) Scheme and additional components of Publicity, Marketing and 
Market promotion (including Export Promotion) Infra structure (inclusive of new 
component of Marketing Complexes / Khadi Plaza). 
 
Features of MPDA are – 
• Production of incentive (PI) plan was approved by t he Commission, as 
modification to existing MDA scheme, to be name as Modified MDA plan  
• Modified MDA plan is financial assistance to Kis re quiring fiscal support to 
increase the competitiveness of Khadi Production by  improving quality as well 
as marketability and at the same time increase the artisan earning 
• MMDA to be calculated @ 30% on prime cost of Khadi i.e. cost directly 
attributable to production of Khadi  
• Under MMDA plan the Kis will have full freedom  to fix the price of the Khadi 
and Khadi Products based on market demand and acceptability  
• 40% of the amount to be distributed among the Khadi  spinners, weavers and 
karyakartas 
• MMDA Plan provides guidelines for gradual phase out  of financial assistance 
for production and marketing support through products segmentation  
• Provides flexibility to Kis to utilize alternate ma rketing channels and leveraging 
professional expertise for sales promotion.   
KVIC has already transferred the wages direct to the Bank accounts of Khadi artisans 
through DBT. The funds released an amount of Rs. 0. 03 crore as on 06.06.2016 
under MPDA. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 The Ministry has not informed how does it calculat e per day per artisan 
wage for the purposes of overall allocation for MPD A and at what rate the 
wages have been transferred by KVIC to direct bank accounts of Khadi 
artisans.  

-93- 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
The Committee also refers to the reply to Rajya Sab ha Question 1189 
(30.7.15) wherein the Ministry has stated “Khadi spinning and weaving is a 
subsidiary activity. The artisans associated with K hadi Institutions are self-
employed persons. They  operate  charkha/looms  depending  u pon  the  free  time  
available  to them. The artisans are paid on piece rate basis i.e . number of hanks of 
yarn spun and  meters  of  cloth  woven.  Hence,  the  wages  of  Khadi   artisans 
are  not  strictly comparable to  minimum daily wages“. The Committee on 
previous occasions during its study visits has inte racted with khadi artisans in 
presence of the representatives of KVIC and had wit nessed the abject drudgery the 
female artisans had to endure practically for long hours daily, to earn an 
uncertain meager daily wage. The Committee is convi nced that regardless  of  the  
structure  of  khadi  sector,  where  artisans  are   employed casually, the artisans 
must be classified as skilled labourer for the purp oses of wage and other benefits 
and thus recommends that to enforce this earnestly,  it should be made mandatory 
condition for the institutions availing MPDA assistance to classify khadi artisans as 
skilled worker for the wage purposes and other benefits. 
(Para 243) 
 
Action Taken:   
 
 KVIC has informed to the Khadi institutions that i t is mandatory condition for 
availing MPDA assistance. To classify the Khadi art isans as skilled worker for the 
wage purposes and other benefits. 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed if KVIC is ensuring that Khadi 
institutions availing assistance under MPDA are pay ing wages as per skilled 
workers.  If so, does not Ministry’s contradict  th e reply for Rajya Sabha         
Q. 1189 (30.7.15) reply in this regard.  
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
The  Committee  while  appreciates  that  more  com prehensive  coverage 
would  be  available  to  khadi  artisans  under  n ew  social  security  schemes,  it 
however notes that no Budgetary provision has been made in this year’s Budget.  

-94- 
 
The  Committee  may  be  informed  by  when  the  m odalities  of  new  
insurance scheme will be finalized and what will be the share  of premium borne by 
the Ministry and the insurance Companies. Whether the M inistry will seek 
supplementary demand for this purpose.  
(Para 245) 
 
 
Action Taken: 
  
 
 A meeting was held under the chairmanship of Chair man, KVIC with 
Ministry officials and LIC of India, wherein following options were agreed upon. 
i) The best option would be to offer the existing AABY  with PMSBY and 
PMJJBY to khadi artisans. 
ii) In the above dispensation, the artisans have to app roach host of agencies, viz. 
LIC of India, and the banks. Arrangement may be evo lved so that settlement 
of all claims for khadi artisans are made through a  single agency preferably 
LIC of India as they have already built relationship with khadi artisans. 
iii) Another option could be enhancing the benefit of AA BY to three times for 
khadi artisans.  
The proposal is under examination for obtaining app roval for one of the above 
options. 
  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
 The Committee may be informed of final Scheme and share of premium 
to be borne by the Ministry and insurance company i n the proposed new 
arrangement.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee in this penultimate year of 12 th  Plan has recommended the 
performance  audit  by  the  CAG  of  several  flag ship  schemes  like  PMEGP, 
Training Institutions and Tool Room and the NMCP fo r the entire plan period till 
2015-16. In addition, the Ministry should have its other schemes internally 
audited. And the salient findings of these audits m ust be included in the Annual 
Report. The Committee’s Reports may become the refe rence for such an audit. 
(Para 247) 
 
 

-95- 
 
Action Taken: 
 
 
Observations of the Committee have been noted for c ompliance.  In case of 
Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS), an Ev aluation Study of the 
Scheme was conducted and final Report submitted on February, 2014 .  
  
An evaluation study of CGTMSE was conducted and fin al report was 
submitted in January, 2014 
 Controller of Accounts of the Ministry will conduc t internal audit for the 
following schemes through two teams of Internal Audit wing for the year 2016-17:  
i. Quality of Technology Support Institutions and Programme 
ii. Infrastructure Development and Capacity Building. 
iii. Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme 
         iv.       Market Development Assistance Programme 
 
The files are being audited by Internal Audit Team of the M/o MSME
